plan.contextChunk: This figure has two panels, (a) and (b), each drawing a convex polygon over labeled points in the plane. In (a) a light gray polygon labeled Q_j fills the right portion; its boundary runs from p_0 at the bottom left up to p_j at the top, right through p_k and two unlabeled black dots, down the right side to p_2, and back along the bottom through p_1 to p_0. A darker gray triangle is attached along the left, with corners p_0, p_j, and a further point p_i lying outside to the left, so that the two shaded regions together form a larger polygon whose boundary now passes through p_i. In (b) the hull boundary is a thick gray chain from p_0 rightward to p_1, up the right side, and back across the top through p_j; at the left a thin-outlined light gray triangle has corners p_i, p_r just to its right, and p_0 at the bottom, and a point p_t sits inside that triangle. Dashed segments join p_i and p_r to p_t, and a small arc marks the angle at p_t. Placing the panels side by side contrasts a point that enlarges the hull with a point enclosed by three others and therefore incapable of being a hull vertex. The pair underpins the correctness argument for Graham's scan, where each newly considered point either joins the stack or forces an earlier point off it.

interactionPlan.concept: Graham's scan keeps only points that make a left turn on the current hull boundary, because a nonleft-turn point is trapped inside a triangle formed by surrounding points and cannot be a convex-hull vertex.

interactions.label: Turn case
interactions.teaches: A left turn places the candidate outside the current hull so it expands the boundary, while a nonleft turn shows a point enclosed by other points and therefore unable to remain on the convex hull

interactions.label: Step Graham-scan stack update
interactions.teaches: The scan repeatedly checks the turn made by the top stack points and the next candidate: left turns are pushed onto the hull, but nonleft turns force the middle point to be removed because it lies inside a triangle formed by its neighbors
Selecting p_i, p_j, p_r, or p_t identifies the local edge or triangle that proves whether that point belongs on the hull boundary or is trapped inside it

demo_steps.title: Candidate outside the current hull
demo_steps.narration: In the left-turn case, p_i lies outside the current polygon Q_j. Adding p_i replaces the edge from p0 to p_j with two outer edges, p0-p_i and p_i-p_j, so the hull grows.

demo_steps.title: Candidate hidden inside a triangle
demo_steps.narration: In the nonleft-turn case, p_t is inside the triangle formed by p_i, p_r, and p0. Since the surrounding triangle already contains it, p_t cannot be an extreme point of the convex hull.

demo_steps.title: Why Graham's scan pops points
demo_steps.narration: When the angle test gives a nonleft turn, the middle point on the stack is not part of the final hull. The algorithm removes it and tests again until the boundary makes a left turn.

demo_steps.title: Local turn, global correctness
demo_steps.narration: The scan does not need to know the final hull in advance: each local left-turn or nonleft-turn test gives enough geometric evidence to push a new hull vertex or delete an interior point.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A nonleft turn proves that the middle point is inside a triangle formed by neighboring points, so it cannot be a vertex of the convex hull.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use two clean black-and-gray convex-hull sketches matching the source: panel (a) on the left and panel (b) on the right, or show one enlarged case at a time under the toggle. Points are small black dots with italic math labels. Hull boundaries are thick medium-gray strokes; proof/helper edges are thinner black or dashed. In the left-turn view, shade Q_j light gray and the added triangle p0-p_i-p_j darker gray to show the hull expansion. In the nonleft-turn view, shade only the small triangle p_i-p_r-p0 light gray, place p_t clearly inside it, draw dashed rays from p_t to p_i and p_r, and mark the angle at p_t with a small arc. The stack-step button should animate highlights on the tested triple of points, then either color the new outer hull edges for a push or fade/cross out the interior point for a pop.

authoredContext: Theorem 33.1 (Correctness of Graham’s scan) If GRAHAM-SCAN executes on a set Q of points, where jQj _x0015_ 3, then at termination, the stack S consists of, from bottom to top, exactly the vertices of CH.Q/ in counterclockwise order. Proof After line 2, we have the sequence of points hp1; p2; : : : ; pmi. Let us define, for i D 2; 3; : : : ; m, the subset of points Qi D fp0; p1; : : : ; pi g. The points in Q Qm are those that were removed because they had the same polar angle relative to p0 as some point in Qm; these points are not in CH.Q/, and so CH.Qm/ D CH.Q/. Thus, it suffices to show that when GRAHAM-SCAN terminates, the stack S consists of the vertices of CH.Qm/ in counterclockwise order, when listed from bottom to top. Note that just as p0, p1, and pm are vertices of CH.Q/, the points p0, p1, and pi are all vertices of CH.Qi/. The proof uses the following loop invariant: At the start of each iteration of the for loop of lines 9–12, stack S consists of, from bottom to top, exactly the vertices of CH.Qi1/ in counterclockwise order
